nameStory: The long-flange millipede gets its name from the distinctive flanges - thin, wing-like projections that extend outward from each body segment like tiny shelves. These flanges are notably longer and more prominent than those found on most other millipedes, giving this species its signature elongated profile.
description: The long-flange millipede is a small, worm-like creature with a segmented body that's typically brownish or grayish in color. Unlike centipedes which have one pair of legs per segment, millipedes have two pairs per segment, giving them their characteristic slow, wave-like movement. This species grows to about 1-2 inches long and has prominent wing-like flanges extending from each body segment. Originally from Southeast Asia, it's been accidentally transported around the world and occasionally shows up in New England.

idTips.label: Long flanges
idTips.description: Look for prominent, shelf-like projections extending horizontally from each body segment - these flanges are longer and more noticeable than on native millipedes

idTips.label: Body segments
idTips.description: Count the segments - each has two pairs of tiny legs underneath and appears as distinct rings around the cylindrical body

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Moves very slowly with a characteristic wave-like rippling motion as hundreds of tiny legs work in coordination

idTips.label: Defense behavior
idTips.description: When disturbed, coils into a tight spiral like a watch spring and may release a slightly sweet, musty odor

idTips.label: Size and color
idTips.description: About as long as a paperclip, with a brownish-gray body that feels smooth and slightly firm to the touch

habitat: In New England, this tropical species would only survive in heated indoor environments like greenhouses, conservatories, or warm basements with high humidity. Look for them in potting soil, compost piles, or around the bases of potted plants where they feed on decaying organic matter.

seasonality.spring: Indoor populations may become more active as temperatures warm and humidity increases in greenhouses and conservatories.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period indoors, when warm humid conditions are most favorable for feeding and reproduction.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues indoors but may slow slightly as outdoor temperatures drop and indoor heating begins.
seasonality.winter: Only survives in consistently heated indoor spaces - would not survive New England's outdoor winter conditions.

funFact: This millipede is one of nature's most successful stowaways - it has hitchhiked around the world in potted plants and cargo, establishing populations on every continent except Antarctica, all from accidental human transport!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with native millipedes, but the long-flange millipede's prominent shelf-like flanges extending from each segment make it distinctive. Native millipedes have much smaller, less noticeable flanges. Remember: long flanges = long-flange millipede.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "millipede" (meaning "thousand feet"), this species actually has far fewer legs - typically around 200-400 depending on the number of body segments. The name is more about the impression of having countless tiny legs than an actual count.
compareHints: As the only Orthomorpha species documented in New England, compare it to native millipede families like flat-backed millipedes (Polydesmidae). The long-flange millipede's flanges extend much further horizontally from the body, and it lacks the more robust, flattened appearance of our native species. Its tropical origin also means it's restricted to indoor heated environments unlike our cold-hardy native millipedes.
